parameters.label: Całkowita masa wyrzuconego materiału (kurtyna wyrzutowa, v>1 km/s)
parameters.locator: artemieva2020 §4.1 & Table 1 (4.8e16 kg); kring2002 §2.1 [9] (>1e4 km3, >25 trillion t)
parameters.notes: Not measured. 4.8e16 kg = ejecta-curtain mass in SOVA vertical-impact model; kring2002 gives >2.5e16 kg as a scaling lower bound. Only a few % of this reaches distal sites.

parameters.label: Objętość materiału przemieszczonego w kraterze przejściowym
parameters.notes: Displaced, not all ejected; >1e4 km3 ejected.

parameters.label: Całkowita objętość stopu skał podłoża
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §4.2
parameters.notes: ~80% remains in/near crater; ~3% ejected beyond rim at >1 km/s. Hydrocode values 2.9–4.9e4 km3 melt and 2.6–8.4e3 km3 vapor (Pierazzo et al. 1998) are quoted in kring2002 §2.1.

parameters.label: Objętość wyrzutów o prędkości >5 km/s (mogących dotrzeć globalnie)
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §4.1, Table 3; morgan2022 Abstract ("several thousand gigatonnes … >5 km/s")
parameters.notes: 770 km3 = standard 45° model (minimum estimate); max for 30° impact. Review states several thousand Gt at >5 km/s.

parameters.label: Masa materiału pióropusza parowego (wyrzuty wysokoenergetyczne)
parameters.method: model:kring2002 (from Pierazzo et al. 1998 hydrocode); model:artemieva2020
parameters.locator: kring2002 §5.1 [40] (1–2.5e16 kg); artemieva2020 §4.1 (~1e14 kg vertical model; 1.6–6.9e14 kg to distal sites for 45–60° wet target)
parameters.notes: Two orders of magnitude disagreement between plume masses used for thermal-pulse calculations; controls re-entry energy.

parameters.label: Grubość dystalnej warstwy K-Pg (>4000–6000 km)
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §1 ("no more than 2–4 mm", >4000 km) & §2.1 (2–3 mm); artemieva2020 §1, §4.1 (~3 mm, >6000 km); gulick2019 Introduction (2–3 mm, >6000 km); smit1999 Abstract (mm-thin)
parameters.notes: Near-constant thickness worldwide; not reproduced by purely ballistic models.

parameters.label: Masa dystalnej warstwy K-Pg
parameters.locator: artemieva2020 §4.1
parameters.notes: ~3e15 kg; microkrystites ~66% → ~2e15 kg (2000 Gt).

parameters.label: Globalna objętość sferul w warstwie K-Pg
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §2.1 (850 km3 of spherules in total clay volume 1000–1500 km3, citing Smit 1999) and §4.1 (model ≥770 km3)
parameters.notes: 850 km3 is quoted from Smit 1999 via artemieva2009 (Smit full text not read).

parameters.label: Masa sferul na jednostkę powierzchni (globalnie)
parameters.locator: toon2016 Table 1 (2.3e18 g; 0.44 g/cm2); robertson2013 [5] and morgan2013 §2.5 [14] (10 kg/m2 used by Melosh et al. 1990)
parameters.notes: Column of re-entering spherules determines both energy deposited and self-shielding.

parameters.label: Grubość osadu zdarzenia K-Pg w odległości ~300–400 km
parameters.locator: schulte2010 SOM Table S1 ("Very proximal … 10 to >80 m")
parameters.notes: Event deposit (breccias, ejecta, flows), not pure ballistic fallout. Value 45 m is a mid-range placeholder; upper bound open-ended (>80 m).

parameters.label: Grubość wyrzutów na wyspie Albion (Belize, 360 km)
parameters.locator: pope1999 Abstract & section "Albion Formation spheroid bed/diamictite bed"
parameters.notes: Basal spheroid bed ~1 m (0.10–1.72 m, up to 4 flows) + diamictite ~15 m (top eroded, original thickness unknown); blocks up to ~8 m.

parameters.label: Grubość osadu zdarzenia K-Pg w odległości ~500–1000 km
parameters.locator: schulte2010 SOM Table S1 ("dm to 10 m"); hildebrand1990 Abstract (Haiti ~50 cm); kring2002 [13] (Haiti ~46 cm); artemieva2009 §2.2 (Beloc 20–30 cm + 20–40 cm)
parameters.notes: Thicker values include tsunami/mass-flow components around the Gulf of Mexico (up to 9 m in smit1999). 0.5 m = Haiti ejecta layer.

parameters.label: Grubość warstwy K-Pg w Ameryce Płn. (2000–4000 km)
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §1 (0.5–2.0 cm, dual layer); kring2002 [13] (Raton Basin 1–2 cm); schulte2010 SOM Table S1 ("Intermediate … 1 to 10 cm"); smit1999 Abstract (cm-thick, 2500–4000 km)
parameters.notes: Dual layer: lower spherule (ejecta-curtain) layer + upper Ir-rich "fireball" layer.

parameters.label: Średnica sferul szklistych ~1000 km (Haiti, Meksyk)
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §2.2 (Beloc 1–6 mm); depalma2019 "Ejecta…" (Beloc avg 3–4 mm up to ≥8 mm; Mimbral 3–5 mm, blebs to 15 mm); kring2002 [14] (Haiti spherical mean 1.25±0.49 mm, lengths to 10 mm)
parameters.notes: Reported averages differ between studies (sample/method dependent).

parameters.label: Średnica sferul ~3000 km (Tanis, Gorgonilla)
parameters.locator: depalma2019 (Tanis 0.3–1.4 mm; Gorgonilla ~1 mm); kring2002 [14] (Wyoming 0.04–1.4 mm, mean 0.90±0.17 mm)

parameters.label: Średnica mikrokrystytów w warstwie dystalnej
parameters.locator: kring2002 [18]–[19] (avg ~250 µm; spinel-bearing 30–500 µm); johnson2012 Abstract (model ~250 µm); artemieva2020 §4.2 (50–250 µm)

parameters.label: Maks. rozmiar ziaren kwarcu szokowego vs odległość (Haiti → N. Zelandia)
parameters.locator: kring2002 Table 1 (Haiti 1250 µm; W. Interior 480–640 µm; Europe 120–190 µm; NZ 110 µm; Pacific mean ≤50 µm); morgan2006 Abstract (gradual decrease with paleodistance)
parameters.notes: Max grain size ~ D^-0.6 (Morgan et al. 2006, as cited in artemieva2009 §5.4).

parameters.label: Globalna objętość kwarcu szokowego w warstwie K-Pg
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §2.1, Table 1
parameters.notes: Distal (>3000 km) part 0.017–0.053 km3.

parameters.label: Wzbogacenie w iryd względem tła (Gubbio / Stevns Klint / N. Zelandia)
parameters.locator: alvarez1980 Abstract
parameters.notes: ~30x Italy, ~160x Denmark, ~20x New Zealand.

parameters.label: Średni strumień irydu w warstwie K-Pg
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §2 (40–55e-9 g/cm2); kring2002 [4] (site range 3–340 ng/cm2)
parameters.notes: Total Ir worldwide 2.0–2.8e8 kg (artemieva2009 §2).

parameters.label: Maks. koncentracja Ir (przykłady: Stevns Klint, Gubbio, Starkville, Tanis)

parameters.label: Udział wyrzutów wysokoenergetycznych uciekających z Ziemi
parameters.locator: kring2002 Abstract, [37] (~12% of plume material); artemieva2009 §4.1 (5% of projectile, standard model)
parameters.notes: Different reference quantities (plume material vs projectile).

parameters.label: Prędkość wejścia wyrzutów w atmosferę
parameters.locator: morgan2013 §4.2 [29] & §5.1 [32] (early ejecta 4–4.5 km/s; mean 4.5/6.5/7.5 km/s proximal/intermediate/distal); kring2002 [40] (~3–11 km/s)

parameters.label: Całkowita energia zdeponowana w atmosferze przez powracające wyrzuty
parameters.locator: kring2002 §5 [38] (~1e13 t at hypervelocity, 4e23–1e24 J); robertson2004 p. 762 (Melosh 1990: 1.3–5e8 J/m2)

parameters.label: Prędkość chmury pyłowej (oddziaływanie kurtyny wyrzutowej z atmosferą)
parameters.locator: artemieva2020 §4.1, Fig. 1 caption
parameters.notes: Up to 3 km/s at >5000 km; >1 km/s at 8000 km after 1 h; 10–30% of curtain mass stays aloft (b=1–1.2).

parameters.label: Rozpad kurtyny wyrzutowej w szybką chmurę pyłową
parameters.locator: artemieva2020 §3, Figs 1–2
parameters.notes: Curtain visible at 300 s, transforming by 600 s; for fine-rich SFD (b=1.2) curtain gone by 300 s.

parameters.label: Czas dotarcia wyrzutów kurtyny na ~1000 km
parameters.method: scaling:flat-Earth ballistic, 45° launch, no drag (computed in this thread)
parameters.locator: Own calculation (v≈3.1 km/s → ~7.5 min); consistent with artemieva2009 §5.5 (ejecta arriving ~1000 km re-enter at ~2 km/s at 100 km altitude)
parameters.notes: NOT a published value — simple ballistic estimate for animation pacing; cross-checks: same method gives ~11 min at 2250 km (morgan2013: ~10 min) and ~13 min at 3050 km (depalma2019: 13–25 min).

parameters.label: Czas dotarcia pierwszych wyrzutów do górnej atmosfery na 2000–2500 km
parameters.locator: morgan2013 §4.2 [29] (~10 min, proximal 2000–2500 km); kring2002 §6 [59] (high-energy ejecta above Colorado 2–3 min; low-energy ejecta ~15 min)
parameters.notes: Kring & Durda assume plume speeds up to 11.2 km/s (power-law), giving earlier arrival; 3D SOVA gives ~10 min.

parameters.label: Czas dotarcia sferul do Tanis (~3050 km)
parameters.locator: depalma2019 "Ejecta, Connection with Chicxulub, and Chronology" and seiche discussion
parameters.notes: Curtain spherules 13–25 min (launch 30–60°), start ~15 min; bulk within 1–2 h; shocked quartz from "warm fireball" ~38 min–2 h. Single-site interpretation.

parameters.label: Czas dotarcia wyrzutów nad Europę / strefę dystalną (7000–8000 km)
parameters.locator: kring2002 [59] (central Europe 18–20 min); morgan2013 §4.2 [29] (distal 7000–8000 km ~33 min)

parameters.label: Czas dotarcia wyrzutów nad antypody
parameters.locator: kring2002 §6 [59] (India 41–42 min; antipode 46 min)
parameters.notes: Antipodal concentration and ~3 daily pulses over 3 days (kring2002 [44]).

parameters.label: Czas globalnego rozprzestrzenienia chmury wyrzutów
parameters.locator: morgan2022 Key points ("within 4–5 hours"); lyons2020 Abstract ("within a few hours"); artemieva2009 §5.5 (several hours, floating-debris mechanism)

parameters.label: Udział wyrzutów wysokoenergetycznych, które powróciły w ciągu 2 h
parameters.locator: kring2002 Abstract, [35]
parameters.notes: ~55% within 8 h, ~85% within 72 h; most within 4 days (Fig. 7).

parameters.label: Udział wyrzutów wysokoenergetycznych, które powróciły w ciągu 8 h
parameters.locator: kring2002 Abstract, [35]

parameters.label: Maksymalny czas lotu balistycznego wyrzutów
parameters.locator: artemieva2009 §5.6
parameters.notes: Non-ballistic redistribution may take several hours; trajectories of some high-energy ejecta reach 50,000–100,000 km (kring2002 [34]).

parameters.label: Czas opadania cząstek ~1 mm z 85 km
parameters.notes: 1 µm particles >1 yr; quartz/spherules hours to a few days; ~250 µm spherules ~12 h through 800–1000 m of water (Caravaca), ~100 µm ~9 days through 5 km (GPC-3) [53].

parameters.label: Czas depozycji całej warstwy K-Pg

disagreements.topic: Magnitude and duration of the re-entry IR pulse at the ground

positions.claim: Global pulse of ~10 kW/m2 (50–150× solar) lasting 1 to several hours, sufficient for global ignition and lethal to unsheltered organisms.
Pulse strong enough to ignite vegetation on several continents (≥12.5 kW/m2 for >20 min), but non-uniform: concentrated near the impact site and antipode, pattern dependent on trajectory.
Self-shielding by settling spherules limits distal surface flux to peaks of 5–15 kW/m2, > solar only ~30 min and >5 kW/m2 for a few minutes.
3D asymmetric ejection: short (minutes) pulses up to ~56 kW/m2 downrange at 2000–5000 km, ~20 kW/m2 distal downrange, negligible uprange beyond 3000 km.
Charcoal record caps ground irradiance in North America at <19 kW/m2 (≤6 kW/m2 for more than a few hours).

disagreements.assessment: Models that include spherule opacity and asymmetric 3D ejection (goldin2009, morgan2013) are more physically complete than the 1990 estimate and agree on minute-scale pulses with strong geographic variability. The hour-long global pulse is best treated as an upper-end, unshielded scenario. Unmodelled factors (reflective submicron dust/vapor cap, translucent spherules) could raise fluxes ~2×, so the issue is not closed.

disagreements.topic: Global vs regional wildfires in the first hours

positions.claim: Global firestorms ignited within hours; soot inventory implies burning of most of the terrestrial biomass.
No distinctive wildfire across North America; charcoal below background and organic matter mostly uncharred.
Fires widespread but not global as a direct result of impact; additional post-impact fires over months.
Proximal fires occurred within minutes to hours (charred trees in Baja California; charcoal in crater fill within the first day).

disagreements.assessment: Proximal fires (≲1000–2500 km, downrange land) are well supported by direct evidence. Instantaneous global ignition is not supported by the self-shielded models or by the North American charcoal record, but cannot be excluded given unmodelled factors; global fires are therefore a contested upper-end scenario for T≤24 h.

disagreements.topic: Source of K-Pg soot and burn markers

positions.claim: Biomass burning in global wildfires; target-rock carbon is 1–2 orders of magnitude too small.
Combustion of hydrocarbons/fossil organic matter at the impact site (carbon cenospheres, pPAH signature, oil-rich target).
Mixed: target-derived black carbon (0.75–2.5 Gt) dispersed globally within hours, plus delayed, protracted wildfires.

disagreements.assessment: The mixed-source view (lyons2020, morgan2013) reconciles the molecular evidence for petrogenic carbon with the large global soot inventory. Target-only estimates (≤~2.6 Gt) fall short of Wolbach-based inventories (~15–70 Gt), so biomass burning remains necessary unless the inventory is overestimated (as morgan2013 §6.3 suggests is possible).

disagreements.topic: Interpretation of low charcoal abundance in North American K-Pg sections

positions.claim: Charcoal 4–8× below background indicates absence of significant wildfires.
Depletion is an artefact of uncorrected sedimentation rate; per unit time charcoal flux was similar to or higher than background; intense firestorms consume charcoal.

disagreements.assessment: The sedimentation-rate argument is quantitatively strong (the K-Pg layer formed in months versus 15–10,000 yr/cm for surrounding sediments), so the charcoal record does not rule out fires; it also does not demonstrate them. Unresolved.

disagreements.topic: Transport mechanism of distal ejecta (ballistic plume condensates vs atmospheric redistribution)

positions.claim: Spherules condensed in the vapor plume and travelled ballistically worldwide, concentrated near crater and antipode.

High-velocity plume mass is too small; ejecta-curtain/atmosphere interaction forms a fast dust cloud (≤3 km/s) and re-entry heating redistributes fines, explaining constant 2–3 mm thickness and distal shocked quartz.

disagreements.assessment: The newer hydrocode results explain more first-order observations (uniform thickness, basement-derived shocked quartz at distal sites), and are adopted in the 2022 review; but they are proof-of-concept (vertical impact, flat Earth, no radiation). Both mechanisms likely contribute.

disagreements.topic: Mass of high-velocity (plume) ejecta driving re-entry heating

positions.claim: 1–2.5×10^16 kg of vapor-plume material (from Pierazzo et al. 1998 hydrocode).
~10^14 kg (vertical) to 1.6–6.9×10^14 kg reaching distal sites (45–60°); 770–1630 km3 at >5 km/s.
Several thousand Gt ejected at >5 km/s.

disagreements.assessment: Values differ by up to two orders of magnitude depending on code, EOS, impact angle and definition (vapor-plume vs all >5 km/s ejecta). The SOVA-based numbers are more recent and tied to observed Ir mass, but definitions must be harmonised before use.

positions.claim: Steeply inclined (45–60°) impact from the northeast (downrange ≈ southwest).
High-angle (>45°) oblique impact with uprange to the southeast (downrange ≈ northwest), from shocked-quartz distribution.

disagreements.assessment: collins2020 is more recent and based on 3D simulations compared with seismic crater structure; morgan2006 is based on one anomalous South Atlantic site. Both agree on a steep (>45°) angle. Direction matters for the thermal-pulse map (morgan2013).

disagreements.topic: Arrival time of first re-entering ejecta at ~2000–2500 km

positions.claim: High-energy ejecta re-enter above Colorado within 2–3 min; low-energy ejecta arrive ~15 min.
First ejecta reach top of atmosphere ~10 min after impact at 2000–2500 km.

disagreements.assessment: Difference stems from the assumed plume velocity distribution (power law up to 11.2 km/s in kring2002 vs hydrocode-derived in morgan2013). The ~10 min value is consistent with simple ballistic estimates for 45° launch and is preferred for the main ejecta mass.

positions.claim: ~1250 km (Toon et al. 1997 Tunguska-calibrated scaling) / ~1500 km (Collins et al. 2005).
Up to 3000 km on a clear day (Shuvalov & Artemieva 2002), reduced to ~2400 km with E^1/6 ignition-threshold scaling.

disagreements.assessment: All are extrapolations ~8 orders of magnitude beyond nuclear-test calibration; a 1000–2400 km band is defensible. Direct evidence (charred trees ~2500 km in Baja California) cannot separate fireball from ejecta re-entry ignition.

openQuestions: No published time-resolved simulation of near-surface air temperature over the first hours coupling fireball radiation, ejecta re-entry and atmospheric dynamics; toon2016 §2.1.1 states the authors are not aware of any simulation of the first few hours. Temperature values in this thread are indirect.
Size-frequency distribution and mass flux of ejecta at the top of the atmosphere are unknown and control self-shielding (morgan2013 §6.1).
Existence and opacity of a submicron dust / rock-vapor / nanoparticle cap above the re-entry layer (could ~double surface flux): johnson2012, toon2016, morgan2013 §6.1.
Impact direction contested (collins2020 NE vs morgan2006 uprange SE); thermal-pulse map depends on it.
Fireball luminous efficiency uncertain over 1e-4–1e-2 (collins2005); fireball durations computed here therefore span ~1–150 min.
Paleodistance of Beloc (Haiti): 500 km in schulte2010 SOM vs 860–910 km in kring2002/artemieva2009 — choose and document one paleogeography.
Ejecta blanket thickness inside ~300 km (from boreholes) not compiled here; a scaling law (McGetchin et al. 1973, cited in kring2002) was not opened — unverified lead.
